answer: In dynamic opportunity-cost bonds, each newly created identity must anchor to an existing identity, incurring costs that increase exponentially with distance in the ledger; this ensures that the expected payoff of Sybil multiplication is strictly negative. Subgame-perfect punishment matrices further reinforce Sybil resistance by imposing ledges of diminishing returns on repeated deviations, forcing rational agents towards a Nash equilibrium where identity multiplicity yields no net benefit, as inefficiencies and pulses of corrective penalties overwhelm potential gains.
